rows.title: Fraud taxonomy and categories
rows.summary: A common taxonomy identifies which actor, scheme, channel, and behavior are involved so the organization can assess, detect, and investigate consistently.
rows.distinction: Chapter 1 classifies risk and fraud parties; Chapter 2 examines behavioral indicators; Chapter 3 develops scheme-specific investigative red flags.
rows.exam: Distinguish the classification of the perpetrator from the specific fraud mechanism.
notes: Classify the actor (internal/external and first/second/third party) separately from the mechanism, channel and victim.
Use a consistent fraud taxonomy when ranking organizational exposure and labelling alert outcomes.
Investigators should test intent and association; transaction patterns alone do not establish the party responsible.
rows.scenario: A bank groups all new-account fraud as identity theft, although some applications use invented data and others use stolen credentials.
rows.best: Separate party classification from fraud mechanism and revisit the taxonomy used in controls and case coding.
traps: Code every scheme involving invented details as third-party identity theft.
Use only the payment channel to determine who committed the fraud.
Merge victim, perpetrator and account holder into one label without evidence.

rows.title: Internal versus external fraud
rows.summary: Fraud sources may be employees or outsiders; insider access and control weakness change both detection and investigative strategy.
rows.distinction: Chapter 1 focuses on organizational exposure and controls; Chapter 3 separates internal fraud schemes and investigation concerns.
rows.exam: A trusted employee misuses legitimate access: assess both insider risk and investigative independence.
notes: Internal fraud uses insider access or trusted positions; external fraud originates outside the organization, although collusion can combine both.
Evaluate access rights, segregation of duties, vendor relationships, and unusual employee behavior as different risk indicators.
An insider investigation needs confidentiality, independence and records of access or approvals.
rows.scenario: A long-serving operations employee approves fictitious loans and redirects proceeds to an outside account.
rows.best: Assess insider misuse and the failed approval controls while preserving an independent investigation.
traps: Treat the transfer as purely external because its beneficiary is outside the bank.
Assume a trusted employee cannot have abused legitimate credentials.
Quietly change permissions without reporting or evaluating the suspicious loans.

rows.title: First-, second-, and third-party fraud
rows.summary: The perpetrator's relationship to the account and victim informs fraud classification, monitoring signals, and evidence assessment.
rows.distinction: Chapter 1 defines the party categories; Chapter 2 relates behavior to fraud indicators; Chapter 3 examines specific schemes such as chargebacks, identity fraud, and money muling.
rows.exam: Do not automatically classify a scheme solely by its name; identify who knowingly acted.
notes: First-party cases involve an actor's own account/information; second-party involves deliberate collaboration; third-party involves unrelated perpetrators.
Money muling may be knowing, coerced or unwitting; determine involvement rather than classifying from payments alone.
Use customer statements, transaction histories and relationships to support the classification.
rows.scenario: An account holder receives proceeds from scams and forwards them, claiming to have believed it was a legitimate job.
rows.best: Investigate knowledge and manipulation before assigning an intentional-collusion label.
traps: Categorize every account used as a mule as intentional second-party fraud.
Assume the account owner is the ultimate architect of the scam.
Close as third-party identity theft because the funds originated elsewhere.

rows.title: Application, origination, and synthetic identity fraud
rows.summary: Application-stage misrepresentation or fabricated identity requires preventive identity checks and investigation of documents and account history.
rows.distinction: Chapter 1 discusses origination vulnerabilities; Chapter 2 addresses identity proofing and data checks; Chapter 3 evaluates application-fraud evidence and red flags.
rows.exam: A seemingly legitimate application can still be fraudulent; distinguish fabricated identity from stolen identity.
notes: Application fraud may use false income, stolen identities or synthetic identities combining genuine and invented data.
Identity proofing, verification of stated information, and cross-checks help reveal discrepancies at origination.
Trace who supplied the application information and whether subsequent borrowing behavior supports intentional deception.
rows.scenario: A lender sees multiple credit applications sharing a genuine address but inconsistent names and identification histories.
rows.best: Assess potential synthetic identity origination and verify the identity attributes and application history.
traps: Treat each application as genuine because one address field matches a real record.
Conclude ordinary identity theft without examining fabricated elements.
Wait for charge-off before assessing the onboarding control gaps.

rows.title: Account takeover and identity theft
rows.summary: Compromised identity or credentials can create suspicious digital activity, unauthorized access, and subsequent fraudulent transactions.
rows.distinction: Chapter 1 outlines identity exposure and controls; Chapter 2 considers devices, biometrics, and channel signals; Chapter 3 examines ATO and identity-fraud investigation.
rows.exam: Decide whether a legitimate customer authorized the activity or their account was compromised.
notes: An account takeover involves unauthorized control of an existing account; identity theft can also facilitate new-account fraud.
Inspect device changes, credential resets, access patterns and beneficiary changes alongside authentication evidence.
Establish who actually initiated activity and whether a legitimate customer consented.
rows.scenario: A customer denies a mobile transfer made after a password reset from a new device.
rows.best: Preserve digital access evidence and test for unauthorized account takeover.
traps: Treat successful login as definitive proof the accountholder initiated the transfer.
Classify the case as an authorized APP scam without examining access records.
Rely solely on transaction size to determine consent.

rows.title: Authorized push payment fraud
rows.summary: APP fraud manipulates an authorized payer; ordinary authentication may confirm the payer without establishing whether the payment is safe.
rows.distinction: Chapter 1 distinguishes APP risks and response obligations; Chapter 2 examines behavioral and channel anomalies; Chapter 3 details the APP typology and social engineering.
rows.exam: Do not assume strong authentication alone prevents an authorized scam payment.
notes: In APP fraud, the victim may personally authorize a transfer because of criminal deception; this differs from account takeover.
Authentication confirms an action or identity but may not establish the legitimacy of the beneficiary or purpose.
Investigate persuasion, communications, new beneficiaries and appropriate reimbursement or recall processes.
rows.scenario: A customer passes all authentication checks but sends funds after a caller impersonates bank security.
rows.best: Consider APP social-engineering indicators rather than closing the case solely because authorization succeeded.
traps: Conclude no fraud because multifactor authentication was completed.
Classify it as account takeover without evidence of compromised account access.
Block all authenticated payments indefinitely instead of applying risk-based controls.

rows.title: Phishing, vishing, smishing, and social engineering
rows.summary: Impersonation and psychological manipulation are methods used to acquire credentials, induce payments, or move victims to another channel.
rows.distinction: Chapter 1 emphasizes exposure and awareness; Chapter 2 examines digital channels and deceptive technologies; Chapter 3 examines tactics and evidence.
rows.exam: Recognize a channel shift or urgent request as part of the attack, not proof of customer wrongdoing.
notes: Phishing typically uses fraudulent messages, vishing voice calls and smishing text messages to deceive victims.
Urgency, authority impersonation and channel switching are risk signals that can be mitigated through staff/customer education and controls.
Collect the communication trail and determine whether it caused credential disclosure or an authorized transfer.
rows.scenario: Several customers receive urgent texts asking them to call a fake bank help desk and then disclose access codes.
rows.best: Connect smishing with follow-on telephone social engineering and account-security controls.
traps: Examine only the original SMS and ignore the later voice channel.
Consider an urgent bank-branded message legitimate unless losses already occurred.
Assume all affected customers intentionally collaborated in the fraud.

2: Use of artificial intelligence to defraud

rows.title: Artificial intelligence and deepfake misuse
rows.summary: AI can strengthen both criminal impersonation and fraud detection, requiring careful identity validation and tailored controls.
rows.distinction: Chapter 1 introduces AI-facilitated crime and protective technology; Chapter 2 describes AI-driven fraud and analytics; Chapter 3 evaluates impersonation schemes.
rows.exam: Separate AI as the means of attack from AI as an analytical defense.
notes: AI is used by criminals for convincing impersonation and by defenders for anomaly recognition; the roles are distinct.
Validate identity through independent channels and assess where voice, image or message authenticity can be spoofed.
A deepfake suspicion requires corroboration, not a conclusive finding based on unusual appearance alone.
rows.scenario: An accounts-payable clerk receives a realistic video request from a supposed executive to change bank details.
rows.best: Independently verify the instruction and examine communication authenticity before release.
traps: Accept the request because facial and voice likeness appear convincing.
Assume AI-assisted fraud can be stopped by transaction amount rules alone.
Treat any use of AI analytics by the bank as evidence that the request is safe.

rows.title: Business email compromise and invoice diversion
rows.summary: Spoofed authority, altered beneficiary information, and urgent invoice instructions link internal payment controls with detection and investigation.
rows.distinction: Chapter 1 treats vendor/payment controls and response; Chapter 2 examines channel-switching patterns; Chapter 3 covers social engineering and document discrepancies.
rows.exam: An authentic-looking invoice with a changed payee requires validation before payment.
notes: Business email compromise exploits impersonation, authority or changed payment instructions; invoice fraud can involve a real vendor.
Separate approval, vendor-master changes and payment processing with appropriate verification and access controls.
Corroborate invoices, beneficiary changes, prior communications and payment trail.
rows.scenario: A regular supplier's invoice arrives with an urgent request to pay a new account.
rows.best: Verify the account change through an independently established supplier contact before payment.
traps: Rely on the familiar invoice template instead of verifying the beneficiary.
Treat finance-team approval alone as proof that new instructions are genuine.
Pay first and investigate only if the supplier later complains.

rows.title: Chargeback and first-party transaction fraud
rows.summary: False disputes require comparing a customer's historical claim pattern with payment and authentication evidence.
rows.distinction: Chapter 1 classifies chargeback/friendly fraud and controls; Chapter 2 examines behavioral patterns; Chapter 3 explains chargeback scheme assessment and card payment rules.
rows.exam: Do not treat every customer chargeback as genuine third-party fraud.
notes: First-party chargeback fraud concerns a customer falsely disputing their own genuine transaction; many chargebacks are legitimate.
Look for patterns of repeated disputes together with authentication, merchant fulfilment and transaction context.
Do not presume customer dishonesty without evaluating evidence and relevant card rules.
rows.scenario: A shopper disputes four delivered orders, while signed delivery records and repeated patterns are available.
rows.best: Review the claim history and supporting transaction evidence before deciding whether the disputes are fraudulent.
traps: Reject every chargeback because the customer has disputed more than once.
Treat a fulfilled order as conclusive proof the cardholder personally purchased it.
Classify the dispute as an account takeover without checking access evidence.

rows.title: Card-not-present and card transaction fraud
rows.summary: Card transaction context, point-of-sale evidence, device signals, and scheme rules support detection and loss recovery decisions.
rows.distinction: Chapter 1 outlines payment exposures and recovery; Chapter 2 assesses transaction signals; Chapter 3 details CNP schemes and card scheme rulebooks.
rows.exam: Distinguish card-present signals from CNP indicators when assessing liability or investigation steps.
notes: Card-not-present fraud differs from card-present activity because the physical payment instrument is absent.
Evaluate card data misuse, merchant attributes, device patterns, transaction velocity and authentication signals.
Investigative conclusions and recovery should consider applicable card-scheme rules and transaction evidence.
rows.scenario: An online merchant shows a burst of purchases using the same device with several unrelated cards.
rows.best: Assess card-not-present patterns and preserve payment, device and merchant records.
traps: Apply only point-of-sale terminal checks to the online transactions.
Assume the device's repeated use proves all cardholders consented.
Consider chargebacks and payment tracing interchangeable investigation steps.

rows.title: Money mules and collusion
rows.summary: Account ownership, intent, coercion, and network connections must be assessed before a mule-related allegation or exit decision.
rows.distinction: Chapter 1 defines intentional and unintentional involvement; Chapter 2 identifies abnormal relationships and patterns; Chapter 3 focuses on mule typologies and exit decisions.
rows.exam: Separate knowing collaboration from an unwitting participant manipulated by criminals.
notes: A mule account can be used to move fraud proceeds; intent and coercion determine whether the holder is a collaborator or victim.
Link analysis can reveal shared beneficiaries, devices and fund flows, but association is not proof of knowing involvement.
Account restrictions or exit should follow evidence, policy and relevant legal duties.
rows.scenario: A student receives numerous small credits from strangers and rapidly transfers them after instructions from an online recruiter.
rows.best: Trace the network and interview the student to assess possible manipulation or knowing mule activity.
traps: Conclude the student planned all underlying scams based only on the pass-through pattern.
Avoid examining transaction links because each transfer is individually small.
Close the account immediately without considering evidence and reporting requirements.

rows.title: Customer behavioral red flags
rows.summary: Unusual behavior is a signal for assessment, not conclusive evidence of fraud; context and corroboration matter.
rows.distinction: Chapter 1 presents red flags in risk assessment; Chapter 2 models behavioral departures; Chapter 3 tests the indicators against case evidence.
rows.exam: A pattern inconsistent with historical behavior warrants review rather than an automatic fraud conclusion.
notes: Customer red flags are deviations requiring context, not automatic determinations of fraud.
Compare activity with a credible behavioral baseline, product use and seasonal context.
Corroborate customer explanations using records rather than treating unusual behavior as deception.
rows.scenario: An elderly customer suddenly sends overseas payments after a new online relationship begins.
rows.best: Assess a possible manipulation pattern and gather corroborating information sensitively.
traps: Conclude confirmed romance fraud without contacting or assessing the customer.
Dismiss the pattern because the account holder personally made the payments.
Treat a single large transfer as proof of first-party fraud.

rows.title: Multi-channel fraud and channel switching
rows.summary: Criminals exploit differences between digital, telephone, and face-to-face touchpoints; linked data can reveal movement across channels.
rows.distinction: Chapter 1 assesses channel risk; Chapter 2 emphasizes channel-switching detection; Chapter 3 examines communication trails and scheme execution.
rows.exam: A fraudster switching from app to call center can exploit inconsistent authentication.
notes: Fraud may move among app, web, call center and face-to-face channels to exploit inconsistent verification.
Link events across channels by time, device, account, contact history and customer identifiers.
Reconstruct the sequence so a telephone reset and mobile transfer are not judged as unrelated.
rows.scenario: A fraudster fails mobile login, calls the help desk to reset access, then executes a transfer online.
rows.best: Correlate cross-channel activity and examine authentication handoffs for a control gap.
traps: Review only the final transfer in isolation.
Assume a successful call-center verification means the earlier failed login is irrelevant.
Manage each channel with unconnected risk labels and independent evidence stores.

rows.title: Investment fraud and victim manipulation
rows.summary: Fraudsters exploit victim trust, urgency, and financial aspirations; identifying manipulation is distinct from detecting unauthorized account access.
rows.distinction: Chapter 1 describes victim vulnerability and recovery limits; Chapter 2 considers behavioral patterns; Chapter 3 examines investment and advance-fee scams.
rows.exam: A victim may authorize a payment while acting under deception.
notes: Investment and advance-fee schemes manipulate trust, returns or urgency; victims may authorize transfers.
Victim susceptibility and unusual transfers are warning indicators, not blame or proof of collusion.
Distinguish deceptive persuasion from unauthorized access when investigating and deciding remediation.
rows.scenario: A customer gradually increases cryptocurrency payments to a platform recommended by a new online contact.
rows.best: Assess possible investment-scam grooming and document the persuasion and payment trail.
traps: Close the case because payments were authorized.
Assume the customer knowingly laundered funds because the destination was crypto-related.
Treat an investment scam as ordinary card-not-present theft without examining the sales narrative.

rows.title: Enterprise fraud risk assessment and detection strategy
rows.summary: Risk assessments identify where fraud controls and analytical models should focus; case findings provide new risk information.
rows.distinction: Chapter 1 details EWRA/RCSA and risk prioritization; Chapter 2 turns risk insights into data/model work; Chapter 3 returns case-based control findings.
rows.exam: Decide whether the next step is risk assessment, rule modification, or investigation based on the problem stated.
notes: Enterprise assessment identifies priority fraud exposures by likelihood, impact, internal/external source and business context.
Review existing controls to identify residual exposure; business RCSA records local risks, controls and action plans.
Use detection and investigation outcomes to update the assessment, not merely to tune individual rules.
rows.scenario: Losses rise in a newly launched instant-payments product despite a low prior risk rating.
rows.best: Reassess fraud exposure and controls, reprioritize mitigation and align analytical detection with the new risk.
traps: Assume the existing risk score remains appropriate until the next yearly review regardless of losses.
Remove low-value alerts immediately without rechecking residual risk.
Treat the detection model's score as the enterprise fraud risk assessment.

deep.title: Risk assessment → detection strategy → investigation findings
deep.lead: A fraud risk assessment decides which threats matter and where the organization should invest. Analytics converts that risk view into measurable detection; investigations reveal whether controls actually worked.

perspectives.question: Which fraud risks must be managed?
perspectives.content: The enterprise-wide fraud risk assessment considers the institution’s size, activities, industry and goals, identifies internal and external schemes, ranks their impact and likelihood, evaluates control effectiveness and residual risk, and assigns mitigation priorities. A line-of-business RCSA records issues, assesses likelihood and impact, assesses control strengths and builds action plans.

perspectives.question: How can data operationalize the identified risks?
perspectives.content: Analysts collect structured and unstructured financial and nonfinancial data, check for discrepancies and unusual behavior, make an initial threat assessment, then use that assessment to support prevention measures and more detailed inquiry. Model requirements should explicitly reflect the risks identified.

perspectives.question: How does an investigation change the risk picture?
perspectives.content: An alert or referral can lead to investigation. Root cause analysis identifies the event’s origin, the sequence that enabled it, and flaws in control design or execution. Findings feed back to risk management so the risk view and control plans stay current.

sections.heading: 1. The assessment is a decision framework, not just a heat map
points: Fraud taxonomy: name the relevant schemes, actors and channels so teams are assessing the same exposure.
Inherent risk: exposure before considering mitigating controls. Residual risk: exposure remaining after assessing those controls.
Risk prioritization: consider impact and likelihood, control effectiveness, and the institution’s risk appetite. Record priorities in a risk register and turn material gaps into action plans.
Ownership: consult business functions and all lines of defense; the guide calls for board approval and independent audit validation of the assessment.

sections.heading: 2. EWRA and RCSA play related, not interchangeable, roles
points: EWRA: considers fraud exposure across the organization and informs investment priorities across products, customers, channels, jurisdictions, staff and vendors.
RCSA: a more granular business-led review documenting risks and issues, assessing their likelihood and impact, rating current controls, and defining owners, timing and resources for remediation.
Assessment cadence: the guide says review the assessment at least annually, and update it as changes in operations, appetite, typologies or actual incidents warrant.

sections.heading: 3. Turning the assessment into detection
points: Translate a prioritized fraud exposure into a detection objective: what behavior would signal that specific threat?

Identify relevant data and validate its quality. In Chapter 2, the initial assessment uses customer records, transactions, internal information and external sources, including both structured and unstructured data.
Select suitable rules or models, set measurable objectives, then evaluate and monitor them. An alert is a lead for assessment, not final proof of fraud.
Keep the risk register and controls under review when detection outcomes show changing patterns or previously unrecognized gaps.

scenario.name: Illustrative scenario: new beneficiary payments
scenario.facts: A bank’s customers have begun sending unusually large instant payments to new beneficiaries. The fraud risk register recognizes account takeover but has not separately considered social-engineered authorized payments. Monitoring alerts are rising, and some customers confirm that they approved transfers after receiving impersonation calls.

steps.label: Chapter 1 — reassess
steps.text: Revisit the fraud taxonomy and channel/product exposures; document the authorized-payment risk, review existing controls, reassess residual risk, and prioritize a response.

steps.label: Chapter 2 — detect
steps.text: Assess new-beneficiary, velocity and behavior signals; review available data and rules; measure alert productivity and avoid unnecessary disruption to legitimate payers.

steps.label: Chapter 3 — investigate
steps.text: Examine individual cases, relevant communications and transaction evidence; determine whether victims were deceived; identify the control gaps that permitted the losses.

scenario.conclusion: Exam distinction: a risk register decides what deserves treatment; a detection model flags transactions; an investigation tests the facts of a specific case. None is a substitute for the others.

mistakes: Treating a model risk score as the organization’s inherent/residual risk assessment.
Assuming a control exists, therefore residual risk is low, without testing its effectiveness.
Treating any suspicious pattern as conclusive proof of fraud.
Updating an alert rule while leaving a newly identified enterprise risk unrecorded.
deep.takeaway: Assess the risk → design and measure the detection → investigate events → update the risk assessment and control response.

rows.title: Inherent risk, residual risk, and control gaps
rows.summary: An exposure is not fully mitigated simply because a control exists; control effectiveness and case failures inform the remaining risk.
rows.distinction: Chapter 1 defines risk assessment mechanics; Chapter 2 tests system and rule performance; Chapter 3 uses root cause findings to reveal gaps.
rows.exam: Distinguish risk before controls from risk remaining after their operation.
notes: Inherent exposure precedes the effect of mitigants; residual exposure remains after evaluating control effectiveness.
A documented control is not necessarily an effective control until design and operation are assessed.
Investigation root causes and failed rules can prompt risk-rating and control reassessment.
rows.scenario: An institution lists dual approval as a mitigant although system logs show one operator can override it.
rows.best: Reevaluate effectiveness and residual risk rather than taking policy documentation at face value.
traps: Classify residual risk as low because the written procedure mandates approval.
Change the inherent risk rating solely because an alert was closed.
Treat an unsuccessful control as evidence no inherent risk exists.

rows.title: Fraud risk appetite and operational thresholds
rows.summary: Risk appetite informs the design of transaction thresholds and escalation criteria, but thresholds require empirical review.
rows.distinction: Chapter 1 sets appetite and prioritization; Chapter 2 evaluates models and rules; Chapter 3 uses thresholds as triggers for case handling.
rows.exam: High alert volume does not by itself prove thresholds are effective.
notes: Fraud risk appetite describes acceptable exposure or loss, while an alert threshold is a specific operational trigger.
Thresholds should be reviewed with loss, alert volumes, precision, false negatives and customer impact.
Investigations establish whether a triggered case warranted action under policies and risk limits.
rows.scenario: A bank lowers an alert threshold and observes far more alerts but no increase in confirmed fraud.
rows.best: Evaluate rule productivity against fraud risk appetite and customer impact before further calibration.
traps: Keep lowering thresholds because more alerts always mean better fraud detection.
Delete the entire rule without assessing missed fraud risk.
Assume alert thresholds and the board's risk appetite are identical concepts.

rows.title: Three lines of defense and independent assurance
rows.summary: The business owns fraud controls, oversight functions set and challenge standards, and independent assurance tests effectiveness, subject to organizational arrangements.
rows.distinction: Chapter 1 details the lines of defense; Chapter 2 addresses model governance and review; Chapter 3 focuses on accountable investigations.
rows.exam: Identify whether a case asks for operational execution, policy oversight, or independent assessment.
notes: The first line commonly executes prevention, detection and response; second line sets policy, monitors and challenges; third line independently assures.
The study guide recognizes organization-specific allocation between the first and second lines.
Model oversight and investigation quality require accountability but are not substitutes for independent assurance.
rows.scenario: A detection team asks the same analysts who designed a rule to certify it independently without challenge.
rows.best: Assign appropriate oversight and independent testing according to the institution's three-line framework.
traps: Call the operational team independent assurance because it built the rule.
Transfer ownership of all fraud investigation decisions to internal audit.
Assume every institution must allocate first- and second-line duties identically.

rows.title: Segregation of duties and insider controls
rows.summary: Concentrated authority creates opportunities for internal fraud; controls and investigative findings should test the actual ability to bypass checks.
rows.distinction: Chapter 1 emphasizes four-eyes controls and access management; Chapter 2 examines validation and penetration testing; Chapter 3 investigates insider schemes and failures.
rows.exam: An approval control is insufficient if the same person can initiate and approve.
notes: Segregation of duties reduces opportunities for one employee to initiate, approve and conceal transactions.
Access, vendor relationships and employee due diligence complement, rather than replace, dual controls.
Investigate misuse of legitimate privileges and examine the actual workflow, not only formal policy.
rows.scenario: A branch officer can create customer loans, approve them and transfer proceeds without review.
rows.best: Identify the concentration of privileges and review suspicious transactions with independent oversight.
traps: Rely on the officer's long service as the principal anti-fraud safeguard.
Consider a monthly audit sufficient to remove the need for maker-checker controls.
Change the employee's job title but leave the system permissions unchanged.

rows.title: Fraud control testing and validation
rows.summary: Testing verifies design and operating effectiveness, while case outcomes reveal blind spots missed by routine validation.
rows.distinction: Chapter 1 uses control tests and audits; Chapter 2 uses model validation and simulated attacks; Chapter 3 identifies control failures and required corrective action.
rows.exam: A control that passes routine tests may still fail against collusion or a new typology.
notes: Control testing must consider design and operating effectiveness; audits and model validation have different scopes.
Stress, penetration and rule reviews can expose weaknesses not visible in ordinary alert statistics.
Findings from actual fraud cases should result in documented remediation and retesting.
rows.scenario: An approved verification control passes paperwork review but is bypassed through repeated call-center resets.
rows.best: Test the operational bypass, assign remediation and verify whether the changed control actually works.
traps: Declare the control effective based solely on documented procedure.
Wait for additional losses rather than examining the demonstrated bypass.
Equate a correctly recorded investigation with proof the underlying preventive control is sound.

rows.title: Regulatory obligations and fraud reporting
rows.summary: Fraud prevention, data handling, case decisions, and external reporting must follow applicable policies and jurisdiction-specific requirements.

rows.exam: Separate internal escalation from regulatory reporting and law-enforcement referral.
notes: Fraud obligations differ by jurisdiction and can involve prevention, customer protection, privacy and suspicious activity reporting.
Reporting internally, to regulators and to law enforcement are distinct decisions with different criteria.
Investigators should follow applicable policy and preserve confidentiality rather than promise blanket disclosure.
rows.scenario: A suspected internal payment diversion triggers operational escalation and a question about external reporting.
rows.best: Use the organization's jurisdiction-specific reporting framework while documenting facts and escalation decisions.
traps: File every possible disclosure to every authority without assessing legal triggers.
Assume an internal incident report always satisfies any external reporting duty.

rows.summary: Fraud teams need useful data but must control access, collection, storage, privacy, corroboration, and retention.
rows.distinction: Chapter 1 establishes data responsibilities; Chapter 2 prepares and models data; Chapter 3 emphasizes lawful collection and defensible evidence handling.
rows.exam: Not all accessible data may lawfully or reliably be used in a case.

Data quality and lawful handling matter when combining external sources, biometrics and transaction history.
Case evidence should be traceable and securely retained according to applicable policy.
rows.scenario: An investigator wants to upload raw customer identity documents to a personal cloud folder for easier analysis.
rows.best: Use approved controlled systems and follow access and retention requirements while preserving evidence.
traps: Prioritize convenience because fraud investigations override ordinary data security controls.
Circulate all records broadly to speed collaboration regardless of need to know.
Delete the original records as soon as a summary is prepared, without checking retention obligations.

rows.title: Fraud training and customer education
rows.summary: Staff and customers must recognize emerging scams, respond effectively, and provide feedback so controls remain usable.
rows.distinction: Chapter 1 designs training and outreach; Chapter 2 measures impacts of fraud controls; Chapter 3 addresses victim communication and case learnings.
rows.exam: Training is a preventive control, not a substitute for monitoring or investigation.
notes: Employee training and customer education help recognize evolving social-engineering and internal-fraud indicators.
Update education based on complaints, incidents and new fraud typologies rather than static annual materials alone.
Awareness is one layer alongside authentication, monitoring, investigation and response.
rows.scenario: Customers report an unfamiliar smishing script while training materials still describe only old email scams.
rows.best: Update relevant training and awareness using the emerging threat alongside operational controls.
traps: Replace all transaction monitoring with customer education.
Keep the training unchanged until losses become large enough for a prosecution.
Assume well-trained customers cannot be deceived by convincing messages.

rows.title: Cross-functional coordination and information sharing
rows.summary: Fraud operations, analytics, risk, AML, legal, and technology must exchange relevant signals and case findings without losing accountability.
rows.distinction: Chapter 1 establishes governance and response roles; Chapter 2 integrates data and specialist input; Chapter 3 structures joint investigations and feedback.
rows.exam: A siloed case is more likely to miss a related transaction, channel, or victim.
notes: Fraud operations, risk, analytics, IT, legal and AML often hold different fragments of a single event.

perspectives.question: What must the control achieve for the organization?
perspectives.content: Controls follow the fraud risk assessment and risk appetite. The guide emphasizes testing and periodic adjustment, balanced against excessive false positives and friction. Real-time rules and models can prompt decisions on suspicious activity.

perspectives.question: How do we build and judge the model?
perspectives.content: Define model requirements, prepare data, engineer features, select and train a model, evaluate it, deploy it and continually refine it. Use confusion-matrix outcomes, precision, recall, specificity, lift and other appropriate measures; conduct tuning and controlled review of rules.

perspectives.question: What happens when the model raises an alert?
perspectives.content: Thresholds reflect policies, exposure, typologies, behavioral patterns and appetite. Triage follows policies and SLAs, with interim risk mitigation if needed; productive alerts warrant investigation. Confirmed case outcomes and gap analysis can justify refinement.

sections.heading: 1. The model-development sequence described in Chapter 2
points: Define requirements: select the fraud risk and objective before choosing the technology.
Acquire and prepare data: gather customer, transaction and known-fraud information; clean and preprocess it.
Engineer features: construct informative indicators, such as unexpected behavioral patterns.
Select and train: pick methods suited to the data and scheme. The guide distinguishes supervised and unsupervised approaches; labeled examples support supervised training.
Evaluate, deploy and refine: assess the selected model, integrate it into operations and periodically monitor performance and new fraud patterns.

sections.heading: 2. Metrics answer different questions
points: True positive (TP): real fraud correctly flagged. False positive (FP): legitimate activity incorrectly flagged.
False negative (FN): real fraud missed. True negative (TN): legitimate activity correctly unflagged.
Precision = TP / (TP + FP): of everything flagged, how much was truly fraud?
Recall or sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN): of all real fraud, how much did we catch?
Specificity = TN / (TN + FP): of all genuine activity, how much did we correctly leave unflagged?
F1: the harmonic mean of precision and recall. Accuracy alone can mislead when fraudulent transactions are rare.

sections.heading: 3. Threshold tuning is a controlled trade-off
points: Lowering a model threshold can catch more fraud but generally brings more false alerts; increasing it can reduce false alerts while missing fraud. The actual outcome depends on model and data.

Training data, validation data and held-out test data have distinct purposes: fitting, tuning and unbiased evaluation. Cross-validation and updated labels help models adapt without relying on training performance alone.
The guide includes below-the-line review of missed fraud and periodic rule performance analysis. Rule changes must be documented, reviewed and approved under model governance.
Chapter 3 completes the link: triage distinguishes productive from nonproductive alerts, identifies interim actions, and sends relevant cases for investigation.

scenario.name: Illustrative scenario: high alert volume
scenario.facts: A fraud monitoring rule was tightened after several account takeover losses. It now catches more suspicious transfers, but large numbers of legitimate customers are challenged and investigators face a backlog.

steps.label: Chapter 1 — balance
steps.text: Review the fraud exposure, the organization’s appetite, and whether the control is proportionate given loss trends and customer friction.

steps.label: Chapter 2 — evaluate
steps.text: Examine precision, recall, false positives and false negatives using validated outcomes; assess whether threshold or feature changes improve performance without hiding missed fraud.

steps.label: Chapter 3 — learn
steps.text: Review productive and nonproductive alerts; examine confirmed case evidence; identify why misses occurred and send validated insights to analytics and risk management.

scenario.conclusion: Exam distinction: more alerts can reflect greater sensitivity, not necessarily better detection quality. Investigative productivity and missed-fraud evidence matter.

mistakes: Assuming precision and recall are identical.
Calling a false positive a fraud that the system failed to catch (that is a false negative).
Judging a rare-fraud model on accuracy alone.
Removing a high-volume rule without understanding missed-fraud exposure and obtaining change approvals.
deep.takeaway: Define and train → assess TP/FP/FN/TN → tune with governance → triage alerts → use case outcomes to recalibrate.

perspectives.question: How does management use the learning?
perspectives.content: Governance and periodic program reviews track fraud losses, incoming cases, false positive rates, customer friction and other measures. An incident may require changes to the risk assessment, controls, training, road map and resource allocation.

perspectives.question: How does analytics use the learning?
perspectives.content: Detection teams use newly labeled outcomes, patterns, rule productivity and missed-fraud evidence to review features, rules, models and thresholds. Updates require testing, documentation and approvals.

perspectives.question: How does a case create actionable feedback?
perspectives.content: The guide explicitly connects an alert to a case, case review, data collection, recommendations and sharing with feedback resolution pillars. Analytics, investigations and risk management translate learning into corrective actions and measurable results.

sections.heading: 1. The investigation-to-improvement chain in Chapter 3
points: Trigger: an alert leads to a case; staff review the event, gather evidence and develop findings.
Explain why: root cause analysis traces the incident’s origin and conditions that allowed it, reviewing control design and execution through repeated “why?” questions.
Recommend: findings identify control gaps and possible immediate or longer-term changes.
Share with resolution pillars: fraud analytics recognizes data patterns; investigators identify causes and gaps; risk management prioritizes strategy, requirements and timelines.
Implement and assess: other responsible teams deploy changes, track defined outcomes and return the results to the cycle.

sections.heading: 2. Not all corrective actions are model tuning
points: If the failure is a model blind spot, analytics may adjust data, features, rules or thresholds.
If the failure is control design, the business might need stronger verification, approvals or segregation of duties.
If the failure is execution, the response may include training, supervision, procedures and accountability.
If the failure is a new or reprioritized typology, the fraud risk assessment, taxonomy, road map and resourcing should be reconsidered.
The Chapter 3 RCA section recommends both immediate and longer-term solutions rather than stopping at the first symptom.

sections.heading: 3. How to tell whether feedback improved the program
points: Monitor fraud write-offs and confirmed losses, incoming fraud cases and fraud basis points to assess the changing loss picture.
Examine false-positive rates and unnecessary customer friction so stronger controls do not impose disproportionate harm on legitimate users.
Track whether action plans are implemented, tested, independently challenged where appropriate and incorporated into the ongoing FRM program review.
Keep leadership reporting and the fraud control road map current. Chapter 1 says mature programs may carry out a full program review annually.

scenario.name: Illustrative scenario: recurring invoice diversion
scenario.facts: A company repeatedly pays falsified vendor invoices because changes to beneficiary bank details are not consistently verified. Fraud investigators recover records and interview the payment staff, identifying weak change validation and insufficient staff awareness.

steps.label: Investigations — establish cause
steps.text: Reconstruct the payment sequence, determine how invoice changes bypassed verification, and document the underlying control design or execution failure.

steps.label: Analytics and risk — select remedies
steps.text: Review rules for changed beneficiary details and recurring anomalies; revise the risk register, assess the remaining exposure and prioritize improvement with accountable owners.

steps.label: Operations — implement and measure
steps.text: Add appropriate validation and staff training, test controls, monitor future fraud losses and false alerts, and report outcomes to management.

scenario.conclusion: Exam distinction: a case conclusion describes what happened; root cause analysis explains why; the feedback loop converts that explanation into improvements that can be tested.

mistakes: Treating case closure as the end of the fraud mitigation process.
Calling the employee’s mistake the final root cause without questioning training, supervision or system design.
Making a control change without an owner, deadline, documentation or outcome measure.
Sending investigation feedback only to analytics when the failure requires business-process changes.
deep.takeaway: Case evidence → root cause and gap analysis → resolution pillars → approved corrective actions → measurement → renewed assessment.

Tell the witness what the investigator believes occurred before asking questions.
Elicit the full communication sequence with neutral questions and corroborate it with records.

Trace the payment and follow relevant recovery or reimbursement processes separately.
Wait for final criminal attribution before preserving payment evidence.

Prepare a defensible incident file and separate any required regulatory report process.
Assume internal management notification automatically meets SAR obligations.
Remove contradictory evidence to make the report more concise.

Identify and correct the systemic reset weakness and evaluate whether remediation is effective.
Close each loss and leave the process unchanged.

questions.explain: Residual risk is assessed after the strength and effectiveness of controls are considered; merely installing a control does not demonstrate effectiveness.

False-negative rate

questions.prompt: A bank lowers its fraud score threshold to detect more suspicious transactions. What is the most plausible trade-off, assuming other conditions remain comparable?
options: Higher recall but potentially more false-positive alerts.
Higher specificity with no possibility of missed fraud.
A guarantee that every flagged transaction is fraudulent.
No effect on customer challenges or investigators.
questions.explain: Chapter 2 states that lower thresholds can increase detections but also false positives; higher thresholds may reduce false positives at the cost of more missed fraud.

questions.prompt: Before deploying a revised fraud model, which THREE actions fit the study guide’s model-management approach?

Use the testing dataset to fit every parameter and report that same result as unbiased.

questions.prompt: A fraud alert generated by a new model is categorized as potentially productive. According to the investigation chapter, which response is most appropriate?

Permanently exit the customer without review.

questions.prompt: After a fraudulent payment, a review concludes that staff failed to verify a changed beneficiary. Which action best demonstrates root cause analysis rather than merely naming a symptom?

Change the fraud loss amount to zero after reimbursement.
Prohibit all customer payments without assessing impact.
questions.explain: Chapter 3 describes repeated “why?” questioning and assessment of control design/execution, followed by immediate and longer-term remedies.

questions.prompt: Investigation feedback shows a recurring new fraud pattern and rising customer complaints from false alerts. Which THREE actions are consistent with the feedback-resolution process?
options: Share case findings with fraud analytics to review emerging patterns and detection tools.

questions.explain: The guide’s feedback pillars include analytics and risk management, while Chapter 1 measures losses, false positives and unnecessary friction.

A requirement that every fraud report be made public.
Automatic proof that the original monitoring rule was accurate.
A new fraud classification unrelated to the identified weakness.
questions.explain: The feedback loop connects case recommendations to owner-led corrective actions with measurable outcomes; a report by itself is not program improvement.

questions.prompt: Which pairing correctly distinguishes root cause analysis from a fraud feedback loop?
